chapter: Philadelphia, Detroit and back to Atlantic City
title: James P. Johnson, Willie the Lion Smith and accompanying singers
summary: He recalls James P. Johnson's burning piano at a matinee and compares Roberts, Johnson, Blake and the Lion as pianists.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: But, I had the chance to meet all the great piano players down there. And that was a -- and then there was another one, James P. Johnson.

At one little affair -- they were all having a great affair, and James P. Johnson came down there with his wife. And he was -- and his wife was a dancer, I don't recall what her name was then, her professional name was Lily Wright. And so she asked Jimmy to play for her, a piece, and she danced. And after she finished, she said, "Jimmy, would you like to play a piece?" Well, Jimmy played a piece. And that broke up the matinee. Because nobody wanted to go near that piano after Jimmy got through playing. The piano was burning up. It was just steaming, see? And so -- and I'll always remember that he played a piece called, "The Bells", or something like that, he called it. But I never heard someone -- Well, all these things intrigued me, you see? Between

Lucky Roberts and James P. Johnson. Oh, they were the greatest for playing, now, for handling a song -- Eubie Blake could play a song behind a singer more legitimately. Along the lines of, but naturally (banging out a rag) for just nicely, (unintelligible), [there] was no comparison, because Art Tatum wasn't on the scene then.

But then, Willy Smith was good, but the only fault with Willy 'the Lion' Smith, was he sometimes -- he loaded the thing so much, that even the singer didn't know where she was half the time. Because he got so far away from the melody, and he was playing these off-chords, that they didn't know where he was. But, on the whole, I got a wealth of knowledge which, I say today, the youngsters can't get. Because, they need to have some more places like that, where things are ad libbed more often, because everything is so formal now, they don't give you a chance to really, you know, get into it and know the bottom of it. And so, that's a failure of the time.
